By the third month, the small bets on the phone game did nothing for Nitin anymore. Only bigger ones made his chest go loose the way the first ones had.
He played in the back of Baba's cloth shop in Jalna, between customers, the screen turned to the wall. When Baba asked where two thousand rupees from the till had gone, Nitin said a supplier had come for an advance. The lie came out so easily that it scared him.
That evening Hafsa messaged: "Volleyball at the maidan? You haven't come in weeks." He wrote back, "Busy with shop accounts." He wasn't.
He lay on the terrace with the phone on his chest, feeling filthy about the till money, and the feeling was so heavy that the only thing that lifted it was one more bet. Dimly, he knew this was going round in a circle.

qa.q: What reason did Nitin give Baba for the missing two thousand rupees?
qa.a: He said a supplier had come for an advance.

qa.q: Why did Nitin place one more bet on the terrace?
qa.a: He felt filthy and ashamed about the till money, and the only thing that lifted that heavy feeling was another bet.

qa.q: What turning point is still available to Nitin now?
qa.a: He could tell Baba or Hafsa the truth about the betting and the money and look for help from a counsellor or support group, since hiding it feeds the shame that drives the next bet.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Nitin's absence from volleyball?
qa.a: Hafsa notices he hasn't come in weeks and gets a short excuse about accounts, so Hafsa may feel shut out or quietly worried.

grounding: Shows a young adult needing bigger bets for the same relief, lying about money, dropping volleyball, and shame from the secrecy driving more betting.

In September, one glass of wine after a long library day had been enough to bring Selin's shoulders down. By December in Rotterdam it took much more, and the calm came later and left sooner.
She began buying from a corner shop two streets away, where nobody from her building went, and kept the bottles in her wardrobe behind her winter boots. When her flatmate Lars asked why she'd missed choir again, she said she had a group assignment. When her mother asked on a video call why she needed extra money this month, she said textbooks.
Each lie sat in her stomach like a stone. At night, alone, she felt ashamed of the wardrobe, and that shame was exactly the feeling she reached for the bottle to quiet.
She had loved choir. She couldn't remember the last song they'd sung.

qa.q: Where did Selin keep the bottles?
qa.a: In her wardrobe behind her winter boots.

qa.q: How does Selin feel about the lies, and how does that feed the pattern?
qa.a: Each lie sits in her stomach like a stone; the shame is exactly what she reaches for the bottle to quiet, so the secrecy keeps the drinking going.

qa.q: What step could break the spiral at this stage?
qa.a: Selin could tell someone she trusts, like Lars or her mother, and speak to a doctor or the student counselling service, because the secrecy is fuelling the shame.

qa.q: What might Lars be noticing from the outside?
qa.a: Lars sees a flatmate who keeps missing choir with excuses and may sense something is wrong without knowing what is hidden.

grounding: Illustrates needing more alcohol for the same calm, hiding it, lying about money and time, dropping choir, and shame from secrecy driving more drinking.

In the small town of Sangli, Vishal used to spend Sundays playing cricket with Tejas and the boys. Now he stayed in his room with his phone, placing bets on a betting app.
At first, small bets had made his worries go quiet. Now small bets did nothing. He needed bigger ones to feel the same rush of relief.
When his mother asked where his salary had gone, he said he'd lent it to a friend. When Tejas asked why he'd missed three matches, he said he had a fever.
Each lie made him feel worse. And feeling worse sent him back to the phone.
One Sunday, Tejas knocked. "Vishal, you look terrible. What's really going on?" Vishal opened his mouth, then closed it.

qa.q: What did Vishal tell his mother about his salary?
qa.a: That he'd lent it to a friend.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling as the lies piled up?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and worse with each lie, and the shame pushed him back to betting.

qa.q: What turning point could open for Vishal when Tejas knocks?
qa.a: Telling Tejas the truth and getting help from family or a counsellor, breaking the secrecy that fuels the spiral.

qa.q: What is Tejas experiencing when he knocks?
qa.a: Tejas seems worried and suspicious, sensing that the fever and missed matches aren't the real story.

grounding: Shows a young man betting more to get the same relief, lying about money and time, dropping cricket, as secrecy and shame drive more use.

passage:
In Warsaw, Yara used to paint on Sunday afternoons. The easel had been folded behind the wardrobe since spring.
Now, most nights, she drank alone in her room. One glass used to calm her down after work. Now it took three, sometimes more, to feel the same.
She hid the bottles in her gym bag and carried them to the recycling bins at night. When Ivan, her flatmate, asked where she'd been, she said, "Walking." When her mother asked why she was short on rent, she said the landlord had raised it.
Every lie made her ashamed. And shame made the evenings harder, which made the glass easier.
One night Ivan found the gym bag. He didn't shout. He sat down beside her.

qa.q: Where did Yara hide the bottles?
qa.a: In her gym bag.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling as the lies built up?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, and that shame made the evenings harder, so she drank more.

qa.q: What turning point does Ivan's calm response offer?
qa.a: It gives Yara a chance to stop hiding and to seek help from someone she trusts or a professional.

qa.q: What is Ivan experiencing when he finds the bag?
qa.a: Ivan is probably shocked and worried, but chooses to stay calm and sit beside her.

grounding: Shows a young woman needing more alcohol for the same relief, hiding it, lying about money and dropping painting, as shame drives use.

passage:
In the college hostel, Yogesh used to be the one organising the chess club. Now he played online games until dawn and missed morning labs.
At first, an hour had helped him forget the pressure. Now even five hours didn't feel enough.
He'd borrowed money from Nandini twice, saying it was for books. It went on game credits. When she asked if he was okay, he said he was just tired.
The chess club met without him. He saw the photos and felt a sting of shame. Then he opened the game again.
On Friday Nandini came to his room with the warden. "Yogesh, we're worried. We're not angry. Can we talk?"

qa.q: What club did Yogesh use to organise?
qa.a: The chess club.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he saw the chess club photos?
qa.a: He felt a sting of shame, and that shame sent him back to the game.

qa.q: What turning point does Nandini create on Friday?
qa.a: Bringing the warden and saying they're worried, not angry, which opens a way to talk and get support.

qa.q: What might Nandini be feeling when she comes with the warden?
qa.a: Nandini is probably worried and uneasy, but determined to help rather than keep his secret.

grounding: Shows a student needing more gaming for the same relief, lying about money, dropping chess, with shame driving more use.

passage:
Farhan,
I'm writing because you asked twice at the fest why I've gone quiet, and I lied both times.
Since the semester started, I've been drinking in my room most nights. It began as a way to take the edge off after the internship rejection. Now it takes more to feel that same loosening, and I hate that I notice. I hide the bottles in my suitcase. I told Amma the extra money she sent was for lab manuals. I told you I was sleeping early on the nights I skipped band practice. I haven't touched my guitar since August.
Every lie makes me feel worse, and feeling worse is exactly when I reach for it. I can see the circle. I just can't step out of it alone.
Tomorrow I have an appointment at the campus wellness centre. I booked it tonight before I could change my mind. Will you come with me and wait outside?
Gopika

qa.q: What did Gopika tell Amma the extra money was for?
qa.a: Lab manuals.

qa.q: What does Gopika mean by "I can see the circle"?
qa.a: Gopika feels ashamed of the lies, and that shame is the very feeling that leads back to drinking.

qa.q: Why is booking the wellness centre appointment an important step?
qa.a: It brings in qualified help and breaks the secrecy that keeps the spiral going, before Gopika can back out.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Farhan may feel worried but also trusted, finally hearing the truth behind the lies and being asked to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult needing more for the same relief, hiding use, lying about money and time and dropping old interests, with shame feeding the spiral.
